READ THE BLUEPRINT
Remember: the <head> describes the page. The <body> contains what people see.
CORE IDEASLearn to read an element.+
<a href="https://example.com"
 class="button">Visit</a>
01 / Element & tag
The whole piece is an element. <a> is its opening tag; </a> closes it.
02 / Attribute
Extra information in the opening tag. Here: href and class.
03 / Value
The information assigned to an attribute: https://example.com and button.
04 / Content
What goes between the tags: Visit. Content can also include other elements.
↳
Some tags travel solo. Void elements such as img, input, br, hr, meta, and link have no content or closing tag.

Small pieces, useful jobs.

No tags found. Try “image”, “heading”, or “input”.

Meaning matters. Semantic tags like <nav>, <main>, and <footer> help people, browsers, and assistive technology understand your page.
GOOD HTML IS A GOOD START.


03
LESS READING. MORE DOING.
See what happens.
Three little experiments.
Go ahead. You can always reset.
A / TEXT & CONTENT
Same words. New meaning.
Headings name a section; paragraphs hold its story. The tag tells the browser which is which.
FIELD RULE Choose headings for structure, not size.
B / LISTS & STRUCTURE
A little order goes a long way.
Use bullets for a collection and numbers when the sequence matters. Each item uses <li>.
TRY / Change the kind of list
FIELD RULE Put each list item inside a list.
C / FORMS & USER INPUT
Start a conversation.
A form groups inputs. Labels tell people what to enter, and a submit button asks the browser to send the form.
TRY / Fill it in, then press Send
FIELD RULE Match each label’s for to the input’s id.
See the complete form code ↗
A FRIENDLY HELLOLOCAL DEMO
Nothing is sent or saved.
A button needs form behavior or JavaScript to perform an action.



  

    UNIQUE ID. REUSABLE CLASS.
    
Classes & IDs.

    
An id identifies one specific element on a page. A class is a reusable label you can apply to many elements—even many cards.
